subject: Civil Engineering
title: Intersection Design
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Intersection Design.

hook.text: Intersections are where most crashes happen. Their design saves or costs lives.

buildup.text: Simple T-intersections work for low traffic. Four-way stops handle moderate volumes.

discovery.text: Turn lanes separate turning vehicles from through traffic — reducing rear-end collisions.

twist.text: Roundabouts eliminate head-on and right-angle crashes — the deadliest collision types.

climax.text: Diverging diamond interchanges cross traffic to the opposite side — counterintuitive but safe.

punchline.text: The safest intersection isn't obvious — it's the one that eliminates conflict.

quiz.question: Why are roundabouts considered safer than traditional intersections?
options: They force drivers to stop completely before entering
They eliminate head-on and right-angle crashes — the deadliest types
They have traffic lights that coordinate flow perfectly

details.summary: Intersection design determines how conflicting traffic movements cross safely by specifying geometry, lane configurations, turn lanes, sight triangles, and pedestrian facilities. Good design minimizes conflict points where vehicle paths cross while maintaining adequate capacity for all movements.
details.whyItMatters: Intersections are where most urban traffic crashes occur. Design choices directly determine safety outcomes, traffic delay, pedestrian accessibility, and neighborhood character.
takeaways: A standard four-leg intersection has 32 vehicle conflict points
Roundabouts reduce conflict points to just 8 compared to conventional intersections
Right-turn channelization and dedicated left-turn lanes reduce conflicts

faq.question: Why are roundabouts safer than traditional signalized intersections?
faq.answer: Roundabouts eliminate head-on and right-angle crashes by forcing all traffic to circulate in one direction at low speeds. They reduce conflict points from 32 to 8 and lower fatal crash rates by approximately 90% compared to conventional intersections.

faq.question: How do engineers determine sight distance requirements at intersections?
faq.answer: Engineers calculate the distance a driver needs to see an approaching vehicle, react, and either stop or safely complete a crossing maneuver. This depends on design speed, driver reaction time, and vehicle acceleration capabilities, then is translated into clear sight triangles.
